transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, doctor. Thank you. Well, honestly, I'm just... I'm at my wit's end, really. What brings me in is, um, I just cannot seem to keep my work in order anymore. I work at a dry cleaner's—doing laundry, pressing, bagging, all of that—and I've been doing it a long time, but right now, my station is just a complete disaster. 

I mean, you have the claim tickets, right? The little pink and yellow slips that go on the hangers. And then the register receipts, and my own workshop notes about which garments need special spot treatments—like if someone brings in a silk blouse with a grease stain or a hem that needs fixing, I have to write that down so I don't forget—and then the actual customer jobs themselves, the heavy clothes in the bins. It's all just... it's all piled together. Just a massive pile. 

I look at my counter and it's this mountain of paper and plastic and fabric, and I just stand there staring at it because I literally do not know what to handle first. I'll pick up a ticket, put it down, pick up a shirt, put it down. It's like my brain just stops working when I look at the mess, but I can't seem to stop making the mess, you know? It used to be I could at least fake my way through the piles, but now I'm losing track of whose coat is whose and where the alteration notes went. And it's embarrassing, really, at my age, 54 years old, to be standing there surrounded by laundry bags and receipts, completely frozen while the bell on the front door is ringing...
Do you feel like your memory has been worse lately?

Honestly? No, I don't really think it's my memory. I mean, if you were to ask me about Mrs. Gable's navy blue peacoat from three weeks ago, I can tell you exactly what it looked like, down to the little anchor design on the buttons and the fact that she had a peppermint wrapper stuffed in the left pocket. I remember all of that perfectly. And I remember all our regulars, I remember their kids' names, I know exactly which chemical solvents to use on, say, a delicate silk versus a heavy wool blend—you can't mix those up, obviously, or you'll ruin the garment, and I never forget those rules. 

So the memory itself, the actual remembering part, is completely fine. It's all up there in my head. I'm 54, so I know sometimes people my age start to worry about, you know, getting older and losing their memory or whatever, but it's really not that. It's more like... I remember that I wrote down the alteration note, and I remember exactly what the note said, but because the physical piece of paper is buried under three pounds of plastic garment bags and a tangled mess of wire hangers, I just can't execute the task. So my brain remembers the information, but my workspace just can't keep up with it, if that makes sense? I'm not forgetting things, I just... I can't find the things once I set them down to actually do the job. So, no, my memory hasn't been worse at all.
Do you find yourself making careless mistakes in your work, such as misplacing garments or forgetting to apply spot treatments?

Careless mistakes? No, no, I really wouldn't say careless. I mean, I never lose the actual clothes. The garments themselves are usually too big to just lose, right? They're on hangers or in the big canvas bins. And I definitely don't forget the spot treatments. Like I was saying before, I know exactly what needs to be done with the stains. 

Just last Tuesday, for instance, Mr. Henderson—he's a regular, comes in every other week—he brought in this beautiful vintage suede jacket. Gorgeous camel color, real delicate, and it had this awful oil stain right on the left lapel. Now, you can't just throw something like that in the standard machine with the regular chemicals, it'll strip the natural oils right out of the leather and ruin it forever. It gets all stiff and cracked. I know that. I knew exactly which specialized leather solvent to use, and I applied it perfectly, let it sit for the exact right amount of time. I'm very, very careful with the actual garments because, well, people trust us with their expensive things, their wedding dresses, their tailored suits, you know? I would never be careless with someone's property. 

It's really just... it's the paperwork around it. The tags, the receipts, the little notes I write to myself. I might put a yellow claim ticket down on the counter instead of pinning it straight to the hanger, and then it gets buried under a pile of plastic garment bags, and then I can't find it to match it to the invoice. But the jacket itself? No, I don't misplace those, and I definitely don't forget the treatments. I'm actually very meticulous about the cleaning part, I really am. It's just my workspace that's a total disaster, so I wouldn't call them careless mistakes, I just... I get stuck in the clutter. Does that make sense?
Do you often feel restless or fidgety at work?

Restless? Fidgety? Um... no, not really. I mean, I'm on my feet all day anyway, right? It's not like I'm sitting at a desk where I'd need to bounce my leg or tap a pencil or whatever it is people do when they're stuck in a chair. In the dry cleaning business, you're always moving. You're walking from the front counter to the racks, you're pulling down the heavy lever on the pressing machine, you're reaching up to hook the finished garments onto the conveyor belt system—you know, the big metal track that spins around when you press the button? 

So I'm constantly in motion, physically. My hands are always busy sorting hangers, folding shirts, bagging dresses. I don't really have time to just stand there and fidget, because there's always a physical task to do. Even when I'm standing at my station staring at that massive pile of paperwork I told you about, the tickets and the receipts and all that, I'm usually holding something. A lint roller, or a tagging gun, or a hanger. 

I guess sometimes I might shift my weight from foot to foot because the anti-fatigue mats we have on the floor are getting a little worn out—they're those thick black rubber ones, but after a few years they start to compress, and standing on concrete for eight hours a day really does a number on your lower back and your knees when you're 54. But that's just normal physical discomfort, right? That's just trying to find a comfortable way to stand while I'm trying to figure out which invoice goes with which pile of clothes. 

So, no, I wouldn't say I feel restless or like I have extra energy I need to burn off or anything like that. I'm usually pretty exhausted by the end of the day from all the walking and lifting. It's just my brain that feels like it's spinning in circles when I look at the mess, but my body is just doing the normal work movements. Does that make sense? I don't think I'm fidgety at all.
Do you feel overwhelmed or anxious when you're standing in front of the messy workspace?

Overwhelmed? Anxious? Um... no, I wouldn't really use those words. I mean, I don't get panic attacks or anything like that. I don't stand there with my heart racing or feeling like the sky is falling. It's not an emotional thing, if that makes sense. 

It's more just... a roadblock. Like, I'll walk up to the front counter—we have this really long laminate counter, it used to have this faux wood grain pattern but it's mostly peeled off near the register from years of sliding heavy winter coats and canvas bags across it—and I'll look at the pile of pink and yellow carbon copy slips. And I know exactly what needs to be done with them. I'm not anxious about the work itself, because I've been doing this forever. I know how to run the register backwards and forwards, I know how to file the claim tickets. 

But when I look at the actual physical pile, it's just like my brain hits a brick wall. It's not anxiety, it's just... I can't figure out which piece of paper to pick up first. It's like all the papers are shouting at the exact same volume. So I might just stand there for a second, kind of staring at it. And then maybe the bell on the front door rings—it's this little brass bell my boss put up back in, oh, it must have been 1998, it has this very distinct, sharp chime—and I'll just immediately move on to helping the customer instead of sorting the pile. 

But I don't feel nervous or scared of the mess. It's just there. It's annoying, sure, because I know I really *should* clear it off, and I want the counter to look nice and professional, but I don't get that tight feeling in my chest that people talk about when they say they have anxiety. I just kind of look at it, realize I don't know where to start, and then end up doing something completely different, like going to the back to refill the plastic wrap rolls on the bagging machine. So, no, I wouldn't say I'm anxious or overwhelmed. Just... stuck, I guess you could call it.
Do you feel frustrated when you're unable to organize your workspace?

Frustrated? Well, no, I wouldn't say frustrated. I mean, frustration implies that I'm getting angry about it, right? Like I'm standing there clenching my fists or wanting to yell at the pile of papers, but it's really not like that at all. It's just... it's just the way my counter looks. 

My boss, Mr. Demetriou—he bought the place back in 2005 from the original owners—now *he* gets frustrated. He'll come out from the back office where he does all the payroll and the bulk ordering for the cleaning solvents and the pressing pads, and he'll look at my station and just shake his head. He'll say how on earth can I find anything in this, and he gets all huffy about it. But for me? No, I don't get mad. 

If I can't organize it, I just sort of... work around it. Like, if the pink claim slips are all mixed up with the safety pins—we use these specialized closed-bottom safety pins so they don't snag the delicate fabrics, especially the silks and the chiffons, you know, because a regular safety pin will just tear a hole right through a silk blouse and then we're buying someone a new two-hundred-dollar shirt—anyway, if the pins are all mixed in with the tags and the loose change from the register, I don't get frustrated. I just sort of push the whole pile over to the left side of the counter, right next to the little glass bowl of peppermints we keep out for the customers, and I clear a tiny little six-inch square of space to write out the new ticket. 

It's more of a... a mild inconvenience, I guess? Like, I know it's messy, and I know I really should put the pins back in their little magnetic tray, and I should file the pink slips in the alphabetical accordion folder. I have the folder right there, it's blue plastic, it's got all the letters on the little tabs. But when I can't bring myself to actually do it, when my brain does that brick wall thing I was telling you about earlier, I don't get upset with myself. I just think, well, I'll get to it later, and I keep moving. Because in this business, you always have to keep moving. The clothes don't stop coming in just because my counter is a disaster. So, no, I don't sit there and stew over it or get frustrated. I just make a little room and keep going. I just don't really have the time or the energy to be frustrated by it, if that makes sense.
Do you ever feel sad or disappointed in yourself because of your inability to organize your workspace?

Sad? Disappointed in myself? Um... no, I wouldn't say that at all. I mean, it's just a messy counter, right? It's not a tragedy. I don't go home at night and cry about a pile of pink carbon slips or a tangled up roll of bagging plastic. 

My husband, Gary—we've been married for thirty-two years this October, actually—he sometimes asks how my day was when I get in, and I'll tell him if we were swamped or if the pressing machine was acting up again, but I never say, "Oh, I'm so depressed because I couldn't put the safety pins away." It's just not something that weighs on my heart like that. I don't beat myself up over it.

I mean, maybe if I actually ruined a garment, then I'd be disappointed in myself. Like, if somebody brought in a vintage silk gown—we get those sometimes from the theater department over at the community college, they bring in these beautiful, delicate pieces from the 1940s that need special spot treatment because you absolutely cannot just throw them in the regular perchloroethylene machine, it would completely destroy the delicate beadwork and probably melt the vintage sequins—if I messed *that* up, or if I lost a customer's favorite suit jacket right before a big job interview, then yes, I'd feel terrible. I would be incredibly disappointed in myself because that really impacts someone's life. 

But my workspace? The loose receipts and the lint rollers and the little plastic collar stays scattered around the register? No. It's just... clutter. It doesn't mean I'm a bad person or that I'm bad at my job. I mean, I know almost all our regular customers by name. I know Mrs. Higgins likes her husband's shirts with heavy starch on the collars and cuffs but light starch on the body, and I know Mr. Abernathy always drops off his golf slacks on Tuesday mornings right after his breakfast at the diner next door. I'm good at what I do. 

The fact that my little area looks like a tornado went through it... well, it's just how it is. It's just paper and plastic. I don't sit there feeling sad about it. When my shift is over, I just punch out at 5:30, grab my purse from the breakroom locker—it's this tiny little rusted metal locker in the back that barely even fits my winter boots, I've been asking Mr. Demetriou to replace them for years—and I just go home and leave it all behind me. So, no, no sadness or anything like that. It's really just a messy counter.
Do you often find it hard to start a task, even when you know what needs to be done?

Hard to start? Um... no, I don't think so. Not if I actually know what needs to be done. If the steps are clear in my head, I just get right to it. I don't sit around putting it off or feeling like I can't begin. 

Like, when I open up the shop at 6:30 in the morning—Mr. Demetriou likes us to open early so people can drop off their suits on their way to the commuter train, the station is just two blocks down the street from us—the very first thing I have to do is turn on the boiler. It's this massive old industrial boiler in the back room, and it takes at least forty-five minutes to build up enough pressure to get the steam going for the pressing machines. If I don't turn that on immediately, the pressers can't do their jobs when they get in at 7:30, and then the whole day is thrown completely off schedule. So I don't ever stand there struggling to start that task. I just walk in, flip the heavy red switch, check the pressure gauge to make sure the water level is right, and then move straight on to emptying the overnight drop box. 

And it's the same with the clothes. If I have a canvas basket of shirts that need to be tagged for the wash line, I know exactly how to do it. I just grab the tagging gun—we use this specific Dennison gun with a fine-fabric needle, and I always make sure to put the little plastic barb right through the manufacturer's care label at the collar, never through the actual fabric, because even a tiny hole can fray after a few trips through the industrial washers—and I just start click-click-clicking away. I don't find it hard to begin. I just do it.

It's really only when things are a disorganized mess, like that pile of papers on my counter I was telling you about, where I *don't* know what the first step should be, that I get that stuck feeling. When I can't figure out the order of things, my brain just halts. But if I know exactly what needs doing? No, I don't have any trouble starting at all. I just jump right in and get to work.
Do you often feel mentally tired after trying to organize your workspace?

Mentally tired? From organizing the counter? Oh, heavens no. I mean, like I was explaining before, I don't really spend enough time actually *trying* to organize it to get tired from it! If I stood there for an hour trying to match up every single stray safety pin with the little magnetic tray, or if I actually sat down and tried sorting all those pink carbon slips by date and last name into that blue accordion folder... well, maybe then my brain would feel a bit fried. 

But I just don't do that. I just push it all to the side so I can write the next ticket. You can't really get mentally exhausted from something you're not really doing, right? I just sort of bypass the whole organizing part altogether.

Now, if you want to talk about what *actually* makes me mentally tired at the shop, it's the end-of-day reconciliation. Mr. Demetriou still uses this ancient Casio cash register—it's this big clunky beige thing from the late nineties, and the keys stick, especially the double-zero key. At 5:15 every evening, I have to run the Z-out report, and then I have to match all the credit card merchant slips—the little white ones that print from the separate Verifone terminal—with the handwritten daily ledger. 

And if we are off by even a few pennies, I have to go back through the entire day's tickets. And remember, we get dozens of people coming in just to pick up a single pair of pants, or maybe they had a coupon for ten percent off a down comforter cleaning, and I have to make sure I punched in the discount code right. *That* makes my brain feel like absolute mush by the time I clock out. Trying to figure out why the drawer is short a dollar fifty when I've had a line out the door since three o'clock... that takes it out of me. 

But the clutter on the counter? The rubber bands and the loose tags? No, looking at that or just sliding it out of the way doesn't drain me at all. I just ignore the mess and focus on the customers. So no, I wouldn't say I get mentally tired from the workspace itself.
Do you find it hard to focus on a single task for a long period of time?

Focusing for a long time? Oh, goodness, yes. That is a completely different story from just starting a task. I can start things just fine, like I said, but staying with it? That’s... well, that’s where the wheels sort of fall off the wagon, I suppose. 

Take the day's dry-cleaning orders, for example. Around two o'clock, things usually quiet down a bit at the shop—the lunch rush of people dropping things off is over, and the evening pickup crowd hasn't started yet—so Mr. Demetriou likes me to go through the yellow carbon copies of all the orders we took in that morning. I'm supposed to make sure the pricing is right and that we didn't miss any special instructions, like if someone wanted a sharp crease in their jeans or absolutely no starch in their collars. 

I can start going over them just fine. I sit on the tall stool behind the register, I get my red pen out, and I'm perfectly focused. For about... oh, maybe three or four minutes. But then, it's like my brain just unhooks itself. I'll be looking right at a ticket, and my eyes are seeing the words, but my mind is suddenly miles and miles away. 

I'll see a note about a blouse, and suddenly I'm thinking about clothing labels, and how half the manufacturers nowadays just slap "Dry Clean Only" on perfectly washable polyester just to cover their own behinds, which honestly is such a waste of our customers' money. And from there, my brain just keeps hopping. Next thing I know, I'm thinking about our choir plans for Sunday—I sing alto in the community Methodist choir, and we're supposed to be learning this new arrangement of "Amazing Grace" that has this really tricky harmony in the third verse that Brenda, our director, insists we can pull off, even though half of us altos can't even read sheet music. Or I'll start worrying about something at home, like whether I remembered to take the pork chops out of the chest freezer in the basement for Gary's dinner, because if they're frozen solid when I get home at six, we'll end up eating scrambled eggs again. 

And then, all of a sudden, I kind of snap back to reality and realize I've just been mindlessly flipping through the stack of orders for ten minutes. I'll look down and realize I missed half of what I was supposed to check. I'll have completely skipped over the upcharges for silk or the notes about missing buttons, and I have to go all the way back to the beginning of the pile and start over. So, yes, sitting there and just keeping my mind on that one single task for a long stretch... it's incredibly hard for me. My mind just wants to go everywhere else.
Do you find it hard to pay attention to one thing for a long time?

Well, yes, exactly! That's just what I was getting at a moment ago. It's exactly like I was saying with those yellow carbon copies for the dry-cleaning orders. 

I can start going over them absolutely fine. I'll sit down, get my red pen—Mr. Demetriou buys these very specific fine-point red pens that I actually quite like, they don't smudge on the carbon paper—and I'll start checking the pricing and the special requests. But keeping my attention on that one thing for a long stretch? Oh, it just doesn't happen. 

After just a few minutes, my mind is completely off on something else. Like I said, I'll be thinking about clothing labels, or what Brenda wants us to do in choir on Sunday, or if I remembered to take something out of the freezer for dinner at home. And the funny thing—well, not funny haha, but you know what I mean—is that my hands will just keep right on working! I'll keep physically flipping through the tickets, maybe even making little checkmarks, but my brain isn't actually paying attention to a single word on the page. 

Then, suddenly, I'll snap out of my little daydream and realize I've missed half of what I was supposed to check. I'll look down and see I completely missed a note about a missing button on a silk blouse, or an upcharge for a heavy winter coat, and I have to gather up the whole pile and go all the way back to where my brain checked out. So, yes, holding my attention on one thing for a long time is incredibly hard for me, even when I'm trying my absolute best to just sit and do the job.
Do you find it hard to keep your mind on one task for as long as it needs to be done?

Well, yes, Doctor, I feel like I'm repeating myself a bit here, but yes, absolutely! It's exactly what I've been trying to explain about those daily dry-cleaning orders. A task like that, it really *needs* to be done all the way through, right to the bottom of the pile, because if I don't finish checking them before the evening rush starts at five o'clock, the whole system gets backed up. 

But keeping my mind on it for the full time it actually takes to finish the job? It just doesn't happen. Like I was just saying, I can start going over them just fine, sitting there with my red pen, feeling very productive. But after a few minutes, my mind is completely off on those silly clothing labels, or Brenda's choir plans, or worrying about what Gary and I are having for dinner at home. 

And then, you know, ten minutes go by, and I snap back and realize I've missed half of what I was supposed to check! The job needs to be done, it has to be finished for Mr. Demetriou, but I'm sitting there daydreaming while my hands are just mindlessly flipping pages. And then I have to go back and do it all over again, which means it takes twice as long as it should have in the first place. So yes, staying with one task until it is completely, fully finished is just... well, it's a monumental struggle for me, it really is.
Do you often get distracted by your surroundings while trying to complete a task?

Distracted by my surroundings? Oh, well... no, actually. Not really. I know that sounds a bit strange, especially after everything I just said about my mind wandering off, but it's the truth. 

When I'm at the shop, for instance, it can get quite loud. We have the big industrial presses hissing, and the conveyor belt clanking around when we're pulling orders, and the bell on the door ringing every time a customer walks in. But none of that really pulls me away from what I'm doing. If I'm trying to check those carbon copies, it's not the hissing of the steam press that distracts me. I don't look up because the door bell rings—well, unless I'm the only one up front, of course, then I have to. But you know what I mean. 

It's not the things *around* me that pull me off track. It's... it's all the things *inside* me. It's my own thoughts! Like I was saying, it's the choir practice, or the pork chops, or the silly clothing labels. I can be in a perfectly quiet room, or I can be right next to the loudest machine in the shop, and the result is exactly the same. My brain just sort of... hijacks itself. So, no, if you're asking if the noise or the people around me are the problem, I'd have to say no. It's really just my own mind going a mile a minute.
Do you find that you can focus on a task for a short period of time, but then your attention starts to wander?

Oh, Doctor, I know I must sound like a broken record today, but yes, that is exactly it! It's like you're pulling the words right out of my mouth, or maybe I just keep saying the exact same thing in different ways. But yes, a short period? I can do that. I can sit down with those yellow dry-cleaning tickets I've been talking about, and for the first two or three minutes, I am absolutely dialed in. 

I'll be checking the names, making sure the starch preferences are marked, looking for any little notes Mr. Demetriou might have scribbled in the margins about a stain. It's completely fine at first! I feel so capable and on top of things. But then... well, it's just like clockwork. Just a few minutes go by, and that short period of focus just completely evaporates. My attention just gets up and walks right out the door. 

Before I even realize it's happening, I'm not really processing the tickets anymore. My eyes are on them, sure, but my brain is off wondering about those scratchy clothing labels again, or trying to remember if Brenda said we were doing the hymns in four-part harmony this Sunday for choir, or if I remembered to take the chicken out to thaw for Gary's dinner at home. And then, just like I was explaining before, I snap back to reality and realize I've gone through ten tickets and missed half of what I was supposed to check! It's never right away, it's always after that little short burst of focus runs out. So yes, a short period is perfectly fine, but then my attention just completely wanders off on its own little vacation.
Do you find it harder to pay attention to a task the longer you work on it?

Oh, goodness, yes, Doctor, and I really, truly apologize because I know I am just saying the exact same thing to you over and over again today! But yes, absolutely, the longer it goes on, the worse it gets. It's exactly like those dry-cleaning orders I keep bringing up. 

When I first sit down with the stack—say it's right after my lunch break, and I've got my red pen, and I'm feeling ready to tackle the afternoon—I can start going over them just fine. The first few minutes are wonderful. I'm checking the dates, I'm looking at the starch requests, I'm making sure Mr. Demetriou's little notes are all accounted for. But the longer I sit there, the harder it gets to keep my brain on the paper. 

After just a few minutes, it's like my mind just gets tired of the tickets and decides to go for a walk. I'll still be flipping the pages, but suddenly I'm thinking about those scratchy labels on the collars, or I'm wondering if Brenda actually booked the church hall for the extra choir practice on Thursday, or I'm stressing about whether I left the porch light on at home for Gary. And the longer I try to push through and keep working, the further away my mind drifts. 

Eventually, I'll just sort of... wake up, I guess you could say, and look down, and I'll realize I've flipped through ten or fifteen tickets and I haven't actually checked a single thing on them! I've missed half of what I was supposed to be looking for because my brain just couldn't hold on to the task any longer. So, yes, the longer I have to sit there and do it, the more impossible it becomes to actually pay attention to what I'm doing. It's so frustrating, because I know I need to get through the whole pile, but my brain just won't let me do it all in one go.
Did you experience similar difficulties with focus, organization, and task completion when you were a child?

Oh, goodness, yes. Yes, I did. You know, it's funny you ask about when I was a child, because I was just talking to Gary about this the other day, well, maybe it was last week, but I was telling him how this isn't exactly a new problem for me. It’s not like I turned fifty and suddenly my brain just decided to stop cooperating, you know? 

Even way back in grade school, I remember... oh, I must have been in Mrs. Gable's class, maybe third grade? Or fourth? I remember she had this big chalkboard, and I was always looking out the window instead of at the board. My teachers, bless their hearts, they were always pulling my mother aside at parent-teacher conferences. I can still picture my mother coming home with that look on her face, setting her purse down on the kitchen table and sighing. They always told her the exact same thing: "She's a bright girl, Mrs. Miller, she really is, but she's just so scattered." That was the word they always used. Scattered. 

And it was true! I was always blurting things out, talking completely out of turn when the teacher was right in the middle of a lesson. I just couldn't seem to hold the thought in my head, it just had to come out right that second. And my desk... oh, my desk was an absolute disaster area. I was constantly losing my assignments, misplacing worksheets, crumbling up important papers at the bottom of my bookbag. My mother used to have to sit with me at the kitchen table every single night and practically hold my hand to get me to finish my homework, because if she didn't constantly remind me to keep working, I'd just drift off and start playing with my pencils or staring at the pattern on the wallpaper. So, yes, to answer your question, this whole... whatever this is, this scattered feeling, it's been with me for as long as I can remember. It's just always been how I am.
Do you experience difficulties with focus and organization at home or in other areas of your life, not just at work?

Oh, it’s everywhere, Doctor. I really, really wish I could say it was just those dry-cleaning tickets at the shop, but it honestly bleeds into absolutely everything I do. And it’s causing some real, tangible problems, it really is. At work... well, I know I've talked your ear off about the shop today, but because of my scattered brain, we've actually had late orders. I'll put a garment in the wrong bin, or I'll lose track of the pickup day, and then the billing... oh my goodness, the billing has gotten so confused lately. I'll mix up the invoices or completely forget to log a payment because I got distracted by the bell on the front door ringing. And that leads to these incredibly tense moments, not just with the other staff who have to scramble to fix my mistakes, but with the customers, too. You can imagine how upset people get when they come in to pick up a suit for a wedding or a funeral and it's not ready, or they think we're overcharging them because my paperwork got all jumbled up. It's just awful, I feel terrible about it every single time it happens.

And then outside of work, like you were asking... well, the exact same thing happens at church. I’ve always been so involved with our congregation, you know, helping with the choir and the events and all of that. But recently, I actually had to step back from leading some of the planning. I was supposed to be organizing the spring fellowship luncheon, and I just... my notes were everywhere, I kept forgetting to call the ladies back about the casseroles, I think I even double-booked the church hall at one point. And I could just tell people were getting so frustrated with me. They were trying to be polite, because it's church, of course, but you can see it in their faces, you know? They’d give me these tight little smiles when I’d show up to a meeting without the sign-up sheets I promised to bring. So I just finally stepped down. I told Brenda she should just take over the planning because I was making a complete mess of it. So yes, it's definitely not just at work, it's really affecting my whole life, and I just hate feeling like I’m constantly letting everyone down no matter where I am.
Have you always had trouble with organization and focus, even as a child, and is it affecting other parts of your life besides work?

Well, like I was just saying a moment ago, yes, that scattered feeling has always, always been there, ever since I was a little girl staring out Mrs. Gable's window. But... and I really should make this clear, because I don't want you to think I've been a complete disaster my entire life! The actual, real trouble—the kind where I'm losing invoices and having to step down from my church committees because I just can't keep anything straight—that hasn't been forever. 

It has really only been causing this level of real trouble for about two years and two months. I know the exact timing, I really do, because that is exactly when I started changing the business into this more complicated boutique model.
